title: A ladder that stops on the third rung
spec: M09 · shadow → canary → expand → full, with an automatic halt
intro: Four stages, 0.0 to 1.00. The bundle clears shadow, clears the 1% canary, and breaches two guardrails at 10% — where on_breach="halt_and_rollback" stops it in 74 seconds. The fourth rung is never reached, and that is the release working.

provenance.source: a narrated progressive rollout of a prior-auth bundle; traffic shares, guardrail readings and determination counts are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This walks M09's Canary With Auto-Halt — the four canary.stage() calls and the canary.guardrails() block that decides whether each one promotes.

steps.title: Stage 1 — shadow, at 0.0 traffic
narrative: canary.stage("shadow", traffic=0.0, duration="24h") is the stage people skip because 0.0 looks like doing nothing. It is doing the most: pa-bundle-v8 processes every real prior-auth request in parallel with v7, its determinations written to the log and acted on by nobody.
Over 24 hours that is 120,000 real requests scored twice. Divergence — the share where v8's decision differs from the one that actually shipped — comes back at 2.4%, under the 5% promotion ceiling.

Shadow catches gross breakage at zero member risk: schema failures, refusals, a prompt that lost its output format. It does not catch subtle quality regressions, because nothing here is graded against truth. That is what the next rung is for.
steps.youDo: Run your next prompt change in shadow for one full traffic cycle before it touches a single live request. It costs inference and buys you the entire class of failures that are obvious in hindsight.

terminal.text: shadow  120,000 requests scored in parallel  live impact: 0 determinations
shadow PASS  divergence 2.4% <= 5.0% ceiling -> promote to canary

steps.title: Stage 2 — 1% live, and the guardrails hold
narrative: Promotion moves 1% of live prior-auth traffic onto v8. At 5,000 determinations an hour that is 50 an hour, and over the six-hour canary window, 300 real members get a determination from the new bundle.

All four guardrails are evaluated continuously against the v7 baseline, not against a fixed number. Auto-deny lands at 0.093 (baseline 0.081, so +0.012 against a +0.03 allowance), override at 0.071 (+0.009 against +0.05), schema-invalid at 0.0017, cost at $0.0101.

Everything is inside its band, so the rollout promotes itself. Notice that the auto-deny rate did move — it is 1.2 points above baseline. On 300 determinations that is roughly four extra denials, which is small enough to be noise and large enough to be the first tick of the needle.
steps.claudeSays: Promotion is a threshold comparison, not a judgement. Every guardrail is within its allowance, so the controller advances the stage without asking anyone.
steps.youDo: Define your guardrails relative to a live baseline rather than as absolute numbers. An auto-deny threshold of '12%' is wrong the moment seasonal mix shifts the baseline.

terminal.text: canary 1%  6h00m  300 determinations issued to live members

auto_deny_rate  0.093  <= baseline 0.081 + 0.03  OK
override_rate   0.071  <= baseline 0.062 + 0.05  OK
schema_invalid  0.0017 <= 0.005                  OK
cost_per_call   0.0101 <= 0.012                  OK

steps.title: Stage 3 — 10%, and two guardrails breach
narrative: At 10% the volume goes up tenfold and the noise floor drops with it. Two hours and 48 minutes in, on 1,400 determinations, the auto-deny rate reads 0.128 — that is +0.047 over baseline against a +0.03 allowance. The override rate breaches in the same window at 0.118, +0.056 against +0.05.
That 1.2-point tick in the canary was not noise. It was the same regression measured on 300 samples instead of 1,400, sitting just inside a threshold that a tenth of the data could not resolve.

on_breach="halt_and_rollback" fires. Traffic goes to zero and the flag reverts to v7 in 74 seconds. No human read a dashboard, and no human needed to: at 500 v8 determinations an hour, every minute of hesitation is another eight members getting a decision from a bundle you already know is wrong.
steps.claudeSays: Two of four guardrails exceeded their allowance in the same evaluation. The controller halted the stage, reverted the flag, and paged. It did not attempt to promote, pause, or ask.
steps.youDo: Compare your guardrail thresholds against the sample size at 1% traffic. A threshold your canary volume cannot statistically resolve is a threshold that promotes bad bundles.

terminal.text:
expand 10%  t+00:41  auto_deny_rate 0.104  OK
expand 10%  t+01:35  auto_deny_rate 0.116  OK
expand 10%  t+02:48  auto_deny_rate 0.128  BREACH
on_breach = halt_and_rollback -> traffic 0.10 -> 0.00, flag reverted to v7
halted in 74s  1,400 determinations issued under v8 at this stage

cells: PASS — the output format was never the problem

steps.title: The rung that was never climbed
narrative: Add up the exposure: 300 determinations at 1% plus 1,400 at 10% is 1,700 members who got a determination from v8. At the excess deny rates each stage actually measured — 1.2 points on the 300, 4.7 points on the 1,400 — that is about 70 wrong denials to re-adjudicate. A batch job, an afternoon, done.

Now price the alternative. A big-bang release over the same eight hours and 48 minutes puts all 44,000 determinations on v8. Same regression, same 4.7 points, 2,068 wrong denials — appeals, letters already mailed, a compliance conversation, and the M11 remediation sweep running for hours.

The ladder is not there to make the release safe. It is there to make the blast radius a number you choose in advance. 1,700 instead of 44,000 is a 96% reduction, and the only reason you got it is that a threshold comparison ran every few minutes while nobody was watching.
steps.claudeSays: The full stage exists in the rollout definition and was never entered. A stage list you always run to the end is a deploy script wearing a canary's name.
steps.youDo: Write down what your current release's blast radius would be if the change were wrong. If the answer is 'everyone', you have a deploy, not a rollout.

terminal.text:
shadow  PASS    0%    120,000 scored, 0 issued
canary  PASS    1%      300 issued
expand  BREACH 10%    1,400 issued  -> halted, rolled back
full    NOT REACHED
handoff -> M11 remediation: re-adjudicate 1,700, expect ~70 changed decisions

items.label: shadow only
items.note: 24h of real requests, zero members affected

view.text: Shadow proves it runs. The canary proves it is not obviously worse. The expand stage is where a real regression finally has enough samples to cross a threshold — so make sure the ladder actually stops there. Guardrails relative to a live baseline, an automatic halt_and_rollback, and a remediation handoff for whatever the exposed cohort was: that is a rollout. Everything else is a deploy with extra steps.
